<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{t11}
Let $d \geqslant 3$, $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded domain 
such that the embedding $W_2^1 (\Omega) \subset L_2 (\Omega)$ is compact.
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{mu3}
\mu_3 < \lambda_1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{t12}
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded doubly connected domain with Lipschitz boundary, 
symmetric with respect to the origin.
In other words,
$\Omega = \Omega_0 \setminus \overline{\Omega_1}$,
where $\overline{\Omega_1} \subset \Omega_0$, and each $\Omega_j$, $j=0,1$, is a bounded simply connected
domain with Lipschitz boundary invariant under the change of variables $x \mapsto -x$.
Then the inequality \eqref{mu3} for the domain $\Omega$ holds true.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{t21}
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded domain.
Then 
$$
\lambda_1 (\Omega) \geqslant \lambda_1 (B_R),
$$
where $B_R$ is a ball of the same volume, $\operatorname{mes}_d B_R = \operatorname{mes}_d \Omega$.
Equality is achieved only in the case of a ball.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{t22}
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded domain.
Then 
$$
\mu_3 (\Omega) \leqslant \mu_2 (B_{\tilde R}),
$$
where $B_{\tilde R}$ is a ball of half volume, $\operatorname{mes}_d B_{\tilde R} = \frac12 \operatorname{mes}_d \Omega$.
Equality is achieved only in the case of two equal balls.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{t23}
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded domain 
such that the embedding $W_2^1 (\Omega) \subset L_2 (\Omega)$ is compact.
Then
$$
\frac{\mu_3 (\Omega)}{\lambda_1 (\Omega)} < \left(\frac{2^{1/d} p_{d,1}'}{j_{\frac{d}2-1}}\right)^2 =: c_d.
$$
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{c24}
In the two-dimensional case
$$
\mu_3 (\Omega) < c_2 \lambda_1 (\Omega), \qquad
c_2 = \frac{2(j_1')^2}{j_0^2} \approx 1,17.
$$
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
If $m\geqslant 1$ and $d\geqslant 3$ then
\begin{equation}
\label{45}
m(m+d-2) \leqslant (p_{d,m}')^2 \leqslant \frac{dm(m+d-2)}{d-2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Clearly, the second term in the numerator of \eqref{ratio} satisfies
$$
\int_0^1 |f(x)|^2 x^{d-3} dx \geqslant \int_0^1|f(x)|^2 x^{d-1} dx ,
$$
and the first inequality \eqref{45} follows.

Next, we substitute $f(x) \equiv 1$ in \eqref{ratio}.
We get
$$
\int_0^1\left(|f'(x)|^2 x^{d-1} + m (m+d-2) |f(x)|^2 x^{d-3}\right) dx
                                 
= \frac{m(m+d-2)}{d-2},
$$
$$
\int_0^1|f(x)|^2 x^{d-1} dx = \frac1d,
$$
which implies the second inequality \eqref{45}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
The lower bound \eqref{45} is just the same as (1'') in \cite{LS}.
The upper bound \eqref{45} is better than (1) in \cite{LS} for $d \geqslant 3$.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{l27}
We have 
$$
j_{\frac{d}2-1} > 2^{1/d} p_{d,1}' 
$$
whenever $d \geqslant 3$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By virtue of \eqref{45} 
\begin{equation}
\label{25}
(p_{d,1}')^2 \leqslant \frac{d(d-1)}{d-2}.
\end{equation}
For zeros of Bessel functions the bound
\begin{equation}
\label{255}
j_\nu \geqslant \nu + |a_1| 2^{-1/3} \nu^{1/3} ,
\end{equation}
is known, see \cite{QuWong}.
Here $a_1$ is the first zero of the Airy function $Ai$, $a_1 \approx - 2,34$.
Therefore, 
$$
j_{\frac{d}2-1} \geqslant \frac{d}2 - 1 + |a_1| 2^{-1/3} \left(\frac{d}2-1\right)^{1/3} 
> \frac{d}2
$$
if $d\geqslant 3$.
So, it suffices to prove that
\begin{equation}
\label{26}
\frac{2^{2/d} (d-1)}{d-2} < \frac{d}4.
\end{equation}
For $d \geqslant 7$ we have
$$
d \geqslant \frac{5d}{d-2} > \frac{5(d-1)}{d-2},
$$
and
$$
2^{2/d} \leqslant 2^{2/7} < \frac54.
$$
Thus, \eqref{26} holds true if $d \geqslant 7$.
For small $d$ we have 
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
d & j_{\frac{d}2-1} & p_{d,1}' \\
\hline
2 & 2,4048 & 1,8412 \\
3 & 3,1416 & 2,0816 \\
4 & 3,8317 & 2,2999 \\
5 & 4,4934 & 2,5011 \\
6 & 5,1356 & 2,6889 \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
We see that 
$$
j_{\frac{d}2-1} > 1,3 \,p_{d,1}' \quad \text{for} \ \ d = 3,4,5,6,
$$
and $2^{1/d} \leqslant 2^{1/3} < 1,3$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
From \eqref{25} and \eqref{255} we see that 
$c_d = O(\frac1d)$, $d \to \infty$.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{l31}
There is a unique solution $\omega_0$ to the Dirichlet problem
$$
\begin{cases}
\Delta \omega_0 = 0 \ \ \text{in} \ \Omega, \\
\left.\omega_0\right|_{\partial\Omega_0} = 0, \ \ \left.\omega_0\right|_{\partial\Omega_1} = 1.
\end{cases}
$$
Moreover, this function is even, $\omega_0 (-x) = \omega_0 (x)$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The existence and the uniqueness of solution to the Dirichlet problem are well known.
The evenness follows from the uniqueness.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{l20}
If $\varphi \in \mathring W_2^1 (\Omega)$, $h \in W_2^1 (U)$, then
\begin{equation*}
            
\int_\Omega \left(\partial_1 \varphi \partial_2 h - \partial_2 \varphi \partial_1 h\right) dx = 0 , \qquad 
\int_\Omega \left(\partial_1 \omega_0 \partial_2 h - \partial_2 \omega_0 \partial_1 h\right) dx = 0 .
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{l32}
Functions
\begin{equation}
\label{31}
\left\{\nabla\varphi_k\right\}_{k=1}^\infty, \quad
\left\{\nabla^\perp\psi_m\right\}_{m=2}^\infty, \quad \nabla \omega_0
\end{equation}
form an orthogonal basis in $L_2 (\Omega, \mathbb{C}^2)$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{l33}
The functions \eqref{31} belong to the space $F (\Omega, \tau)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Clearly, $\operatorname{curl} u, \operatorname{div} u \in L_2 (\Omega)$ for each function $u$ from the set \eqref{31}.
Let us check the boundary condition.
Let $h \in W_2^1 (\Omega)$.
We have
$$
\int_\Omega \operatorname{curl} (\nabla \varphi_k) h\, dx = 0
= \int_\Omega \left(\partial_1 \varphi_k \partial_2 h - \partial_2 \varphi_k \partial_1 h\right) dx
$$
due to Lemma \ref{l20}.
Next,
$$
\int_\Omega \operatorname{curl} (\nabla^\perp \psi_m) h \, dx = - \int_\Omega \Delta \psi_m h \, dx,
$$
and
$$
\int_\Omega \left(\partial_2 \psi_m \partial_2 h + \partial_1 \psi_m \partial_1 h\right) dx = - \int_\Omega \Delta \psi_m h \, dx,
$$
as the function $\psi_m$ is an eigenfunction of the Neumann problem.
Finally,
$$
\int_\Omega \operatorname{curl} (\nabla \omega_0) h\, dx = 0 = \int_\Omega \left(\partial_1 \omega_0 \partial_2 h - \partial_2 \omega_0 \partial_1 h\right) dx
$$
again due to Lemma \ref{l20}.
Thus, \eqref{32} is valid for all functions \eqref{31}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{l34}
The functions \eqref{31} are orhtogonal with respect to the form $a[\cdot, \cdot]$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We have
$$
a [\nabla\varphi_k, \nabla \varphi_l] = \int_\Omega \Delta \varphi_k \Delta \varphi_l dx = 0, \qquad \text{if} \ k \neq l,
$$
$$
a [\nabla^\perp \psi_m, \nabla^\perp \psi_l] = \int_\Omega \Delta \psi_m \Delta \psi_l dx = 0, \qquad \text{if} \ m \neq l.
$$
It is also clear that 
$a [ \nabla\varphi, \nabla^\perp \psi] = 0$ for all $\varphi, \psi \in W_2^1 (\Omega)$,
and $a [u, \nabla \omega_0] = 0$ for all $u \in F (\Omega, \tau)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{l35}
Vector-functions
$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc} \varphi_1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right), \quad
\left(\begin{array}{cc} 0 \\ \varphi_1 \end{array}\right), \quad
\nabla \varphi_1, \quad \nabla \omega_0
$$
belong to the space $F (\Omega, \tau)$, and are orthogonal in $L_2 (\Omega, \mathbb{C}^2)$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Clearly, these vectors belong to $F (\Omega, \tau)$.
We have also
\begin{equation}
\label{34}
\int_\Omega \varphi_1 \partial_j \varphi_1 dx = \frac12 \int_\Omega \partial_j \left(\varphi_1\right)^2 dx = 0,
\quad j = 1,2,
\end{equation}
thus, first three vectors are mutually orthogonal in $L_2$.
Furthermore, $(\nabla \varphi_1, \nabla \omega_0) = 0$.

The eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ is simple,
and function $\varphi_1 (-x)$ is also an eigenfunction for the Dirichlet problem.
Therefore, this function is even, $\varphi_1 (-x) = \varphi_1 (x)$.
The derivative $\partial_j \omega_0$ is odd, $\partial_j \omega_0 (-x) = - \partial_j \omega_0 (x)$
by virtue of Lemma \ref{l31}.
So,
$$
\int_\Omega \varphi_1 (x) \partial_j \omega_0 (x) \, dx = 0, \quad j = 1,2.
\qquad \qedhere
$$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{l36}
We have
$$
L_0 \cap \nabla^\perp \ker\left(-\Delta_N - \lambda_1 I\right) = \{0\}.
$$
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $\nabla^\perp \psi_m \in L_0$.
Lemma \ref{l32} yields that
$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc} \partial_2 \psi_m \\ -\partial_1 \psi_m \end{array}\right)
=  \left(\begin{array}{cc} c_1 \varphi_1 \\ c_2 \varphi_1 \end{array}\right)
$$
with some constants $c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}$.
Assume that $c_1^2 + c_2^2 > 0$.
Introduce new variables $y$ via the formulas
$$
x_1 = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2, \quad x_2 = c_2 y_1 - c_1 y_2.
$$
Then
$$
\frac{\partial\psi_m}{\partial y_1} = c_1 \partial_1 \psi_m + c_2 \partial_2 \psi_m = 0,
$$
and
$$
\frac{\partial\psi_m}{\partial y_2} = c_2 \partial_1 \psi_m - c_1 \partial_2 \psi_m =
- \left(c_1^2 + c_2^2\right) \varphi_1.
$$
The function $\psi_m$ does not depend on $y_1$,
therefore, the functions $\frac{\partial \psi_m}{\partial y_2}$ and $\varphi_1$
do not depend on $y_1$ either.
Now, Dirichlet condition for $\varphi_1$ implies $\varphi_1 \equiv 0$,
and we have a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
$\dim L = \dim \ker\left(-\Delta_N - \lambda_1 I\right) + 4$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{l37}
If $v \in L$ then $a[v] \leqslant \lambda_1 \|v\|_{L_2}^2$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let 
$$
v(x) =  \left(\begin{array}{cc} c_1 \varphi_1 (x) \\ c_2 \varphi_1 (x) \end{array}\right)
+ c_3 \nabla \varphi_1 (x) + c_4 \nabla \omega_0 (x) + \nabla^\perp \psi (x),
$$
where $\psi$ is an eigenfunction of the Neumann problem, 
$- \Delta_N \psi = \lambda_1 \psi$.
Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
\|v\|^2 
= \left(|c_1|^2 + |c_2|^2\right) \|\varphi_1\|^2
+ |c_3|^2 \|\nabla \varphi_1\|^2 + |c_4|^2 \|\nabla \omega_0\|^2 + \|\nabla^\perp \psi\|^2 \\
+ 2 \operatorname{Re} \left(\left(\begin{array}{cc} c_1 \varphi_1 (x) \\ c_2 \varphi_1 (x) \end{array}\right),
\left(\begin{array}{cc} \partial_2 \psi \\ - \partial_1 \psi \end{array}\right)\right) \\
= \left(|c_1|^2 + |c_2|^2 + \lambda_1 |c_3|^2\right) \|\varphi_1\|^2
+ |c_4|^2 \|\nabla \omega_0\|^2 
+ \lambda_1 \|\psi\|^2 + 
2 \operatorname{Re} \int_\Omega \varphi_1 \left(c_1 \overline{\partial_2 \psi} - c_2 \overline{\partial_1 \psi}\right) dx.
\end{eqnarray*}
We have
$$
\operatorname{curl} v = c_2 \partial_1 \varphi_1 - c_1 \partial_2 \varphi_1 + \lambda_1 \psi,
\qquad 
\operatorname{div} v = c_1 \partial_1 \varphi_1 + c_2 \partial_2 \varphi_1 - c_3 \lambda_1 \varphi_1.
$$
Therefore,
\begin{eqnarray*}
a[v] 
= \int_\Omega \left(\left|c_2 \partial_1 \varphi_1 - c_1 \partial_2 \varphi_1 + \lambda_1 \psi\right|^2
+ \left|c_1 \partial_1 \varphi_1 + c_2 \partial_2 \varphi_1 - c_3 \lambda_1 \varphi_1\right|^2\right) dx \\
= \left(|c_1|^2 + |c_2|^2\right) \|\nabla\varphi_1\|^2 + \lambda_1^2 \|\psi\|^2 + 
2 \lambda_1 \operatorname{Re} \int_\Omega \left(c_2 \partial_1 \varphi_1 - c_1 \partial_2 \varphi_1\right) \overline \psi\, dx
+ |c_3|^2 \lambda_1^2 \|\varphi_1\|^2,
\end{eqnarray*}
where we took into account \eqref{34}.
Furthermore,
$$
\int_\Omega \left(c_2 \partial_1 \varphi_1 - c_1 \partial_2 \varphi_1\right) \overline \psi\, dx
= \int_\Omega \varphi_1 \left(c_1 \overline{\partial_2 \psi} - c_2 \overline{\partial_1 \psi}\right) dx,
$$
because $\left.\varphi_1\right|_{\partial\Omega} = 0$.
Therefore,
$$
a[v] = \lambda_1 \left(|c_1|^2 + |c_2|^2 + \lambda_1 |c_3|^2\right) \|\varphi_1\|^2
+ \lambda_1^2 \|\psi\|^2 + 
2 \lambda_1 \operatorname{Re} \int_\Omega \varphi_1 \left(c_1 \overline{\partial_2 \psi} - c_2 \overline{\partial_1 \psi}\right) dx,
$$
and $a[v] \leqslant \lambda_1 \|v\|^2$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
We would consider the space 
$$
F(\Omega, \nu) = \left\{ u \in L_2 (\Omega, \mathbb{C}^2) : \operatorname{div} u, \operatorname{curl} u \in L_2 (\Omega), 
\left. u_\nu\right|_{\partial\Omega} = 0 \right\}
$$
instead of $F(\Omega, \tau)$. 
The choice of the space has no importance
because they transforms one into another by the 90 degree rotation of vectors.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
